match.reason: The closest bank points cover restraining forces only as part of a wider model (force field analysis) or as one kind of resistance, while this point asks for the broader set of blockers, including lack of time, organisational inertia and laws, so no single card teaches it exactly.

draft.title: Restraining forces against change
card: A restraining force is anything that holds a change back or slows it down. A business can face several at once.
People
managers and employees may resist a change. They may fear losing their jobs, dislike new routines or doubt that the change is needed.
Time and inertia
a lack of time can delay a change when staff are busy with daily work. Organisational inertia is the tendency of a business to keep doing things the way it always has.
Laws and cost
laws can limit what a business is allowed to do, so a change may need to be altered or dropped. A change can also cost too much in money, training or lost output.
draft.remember: Restraining forces are the people, time, habit, legal and money barriers that can slow or block a change.

a.q: A bakery's owner wants to introduce new ovens. Staff say, "We have always baked this way and it works." Which restraining force is most clearly shown?
opts: A legal limit on the change
A lack of money for the change
a.why: Staff are keeping to the usual way of working, which is organisational inertia. It is not a legal limit or a cost issue, because neither is mentioned. A competitor would be a force pushing for change, not holding it back.
a.clue: Look for the habit of doing things the old way.

b.q: Priya manages a Geelong clothing chain. She plans a new online ordering system. Staff support it, but the system's price is more than the budget allows. What is the restraining force?
b.why: The only thing holding the change back is that it costs more than the business can afford. Staff support it, so resistance is ruled out. Inertia is also unlikely, because nothing suggests a habit of keeping old methods.
b.clue: Check who supports the change, then find what still blocks it.

problems.detail: The clue 'Look for the habit of doing things the old way' nearly restates the card's definition of organisational inertia. A student can match the clue to the term without applying the idea to the bakery scenario.

a.q: A bakery bought new ovens a year ago. Staff agree they are better and have been trained, yet most batches still go into the old ovens. Which restraining force is most clearly shown?
opts: A legal limit on the change
A lack of money for the change
a.why: No one objects, and the ovens are paid for, so the old way carries on simply because it is what the bakery is used to. That is organisational inertia. A competitor would be a force pushing for change, not holding it back.
a.clue: Nobody objects, so what keeps the old method going?
